preamble: Loss of breathy voice turns [dʱ] into plain [d]. This is one of the most common fates of the Proto-Indo-European voiced aspirates: Iranian, Balto-Slavic, Celtic and Albanian all merged *dʰ with *d, and Germanic arrived at d initially via a fricative stage [ð]. Within Indo-Aryan, which otherwise preserves dʱ, it occurs as dissimilation under Grassmann's Law in Sanskrit and as a wholesale loss of aspiration in Sinhala.

examples.note: Grassmann's Law: the first of two aspirates in successive syllables loses its aspiration, so the reduplicating syllable has d.
Proto-Balto-Slavic *dū́ˀmas; Proto-Slavic *dỳmъ shows the same d.

examples.to: Younger Avestan duuarəm (acc. sg.), Old Persian duvarayā (loc. sg.)
examples.note: Iranian merged the voiced aspirates with the plain voiced stops; Persian dar 'door' continues the form.
Sinhala lost aspiration contrasts entirely; contrast Hindi dhuā̃ and Punjabi dhū̃ 'smoke'.

sources: Turner, R. L. (1962–1966). A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages, entry 6849 dhūmá. https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/soas_query.py?qs=dhUma&searchhws=yes
